name: Winisk River Oji-Cree

catalog_quote: The rhythmic innovations of Oji-Cree lie in the development of left-headed (trochaic) rather than right-headed (iambic) feet, and the alignment of rhythmic structure with the beginning of the grammatical word stem, disregarding prefixes. Primary stress typically falls on the prominent syllable of the last complete foot. In other respects, the system retains the patterns characteristic of Ojibwe: it is quantity-sensitive, treats the final syllable as “extrametrical,” and organizes syllables into feet from left to right (Kaye 1973, as summarized in Valentine 2001). ... (1) 1. the final syllable of a phonological word is always rhythmically strong (is “extrametrical”) 2. all syllables containing a long vowel are rhythmically strong 3. syllables are organized into trochaic feet starting from the beginning of the stem ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive rhythmic system: every long-vowel syllable and the word-final syllable carry a beat; remaining syllables are parsed left-to-right into trochaic (left-headed) feet (HL), (LL), or (H), starting at the left edge of the stem (person prefixes are outside the domain). Per the abstract, primary stress falls on the head of the last complete foot; per the delivered talk's summary slide, there is no single culminative primary word stress and the main pitch prominence is phrasal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: All foot heads, all long-vowel syllables and the final syllable are 'rhythmically strong' (beats); strings of light syllables yield triplet-like rhythms; lapses of two unstressed syllables are tolerated to avoid clash (talk summary).
new_statements.exceptions: Person prefixes are non-cohering (excluded from the foot domain), so stem rhythm stays constant under prefixation; 'typically' hedges the primary-stress statement; the talk's Summary slide (18:20) states 'Oji-Cree is primarily a rhythm-stress language, without a single culminative primary stress on each word' and 'Phrasal pitch prominence is assigned independently from word rhythm, and can occur on a rhythmically weak syllable' — i.e. the author's own delivered version withdraws/qualifies the abstract's culminative primary-stress claim. Valentine 1996 p.314 independently reports Severn 'stress shifts in sequences of short vowels' (mákizin, mínigok, ikído, gakína, nigámo, awíya...).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of footing = phonological word stem (left edge of lexical-grammatical stem), tense/person prefixes outside; final-syllable beat is per phonological word; culminative prominence, if any, is described as phrasal (boundary tones/phrasal pitch) rather than lexical. Based on elicited wordlist (~150 items adapted from Valentine 1996), natural-speech corpus, and Praat verification, Kingfisher Lake (Winisk River) speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Winisk River (eastern) Oji-Cree as spoken at Kingfisher Lake, Ontario (Windsor's title: 'Winisk River Oji-Cree'; his map separates Eastern/Winisk River, Western/Severn River and Southwestern/Severn headwaters community groups). This is a sub-variety of Glottolog seve1240 Severn Ojibwa (iso ojs); Glottolog lists Winisk River and Severn River sub-dialects under seve1240 (sub-codes not verified here). Valentine 1996's stress-shift wordlist is from an unnamed 'Severn Ojibwe speaker'. Note the prosodic system described (trochaic, stem-aligned, no culminative word stress per the talk) differs from the iambic system coded for southern Ojibwe varieties (otta1242 etc.), so seve1240 should not inherit a generic 'Ojibwe' coding.

sources.note: Oji-Cree has developed left-headed (trochaic) QS feet built L-to-R from the beginning of the stem (prefixes excluded); final syllable always rhythmically strong ('extrametrical'); long-vowel syllables always strong; 'Primary stress typically falls on the prominent syllable of the last complete foot'; triplet-like rhythms in strings of light syllables.

sources.note: General Ojibwe: QS iambic feet from the left edge, final syllable often extrametrical; 'The stress system of northern dialects remains to be worked out, though much information can be found in Valentine (1994)' (p.313); p.314: 'Some dialects, notably those in northern Ontario, show stress shifts in sequences of short vowels', with a Severn Ojibwe speaker's forms mákizin, mínigok, mígine, míngizi, mánijoosh, ikído, gakína, nigámo, awíya, inakwázhiwe, ikwaamájiwe. No rule for Severn.
